chapters.title: Chapter 2: The One-Step and Multi-Step Binomial Tree

lessons.title: Extending to Multiple Steps: The Recombining Binomial Tree

children.text: Lessons 1 and 2 nailed down the one-step formula and proved it is the only arbitrage-free price. A real option, Chapter 1's 6-month Nifty put split into 126 daily steps, needs that formula chained across many steps, not just one. Chain it the naive way and the computation explodes before it becomes useful. There is a specific structural property of the binomial tree that prevents that explosion, and it is the whole reason this method is computationally practical at all.
The Naive Approach: A Combinatorial Explosion

If every step genuinely produced two brand-new, independent branches, unrelated to any other branch, then after N steps there would be 2 to the power N distinct terminal outcomes. That sounds manageable for a handful of steps. It stops being manageable almost immediately.

stats.label: After 126 steps
stats.context: 2^126, Chapter 1's 6-month, one-trading-day-per-step example. This is roughly 200 quintillion times the number of seconds since the Big Bang

markDefs.definition: A binomial tree in which the same up and down factors apply at every step regardless of path history, so an up-move followed by a down-move lands on the exact same price as a down-move followed by an up-move. This is what keeps the tree computationally manageable.

children.text: The escape from that explosion is a single modelling choice made back in Lesson 1: the same u and d apply at every step, regardless of what happened before. Multiplication does not care about order, S0 times u times d lands on exactly the same price as S0 times d times u. An up-move followed by a down-move and a down-move followed by an up-move arrive at the identical stock price. Paths that started out different merge back together. This is what a
means, and it is not a simplification made for convenience, it falls straight out of using constant, path-independent up and down factors.

body.latex: S_{N,j} = S_0\, u^{\,j}\, d^{\,N-j}, \qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots, N
body.caption: The stock price after N steps, having gone up on exactly j of them, in any order. Only the count of up-moves matters, never their sequence.

children.text: Because only the count j matters, not the order, there are only N plus 1 distinct terminal prices after N steps, not 2 to the power N. That single fact is what turns an impossible computation into a routine one.

body.caption: Non-recombining branches vs recombining terminal nodes

children.text: With the lattice built, pricing follows three moves. Compute the N plus 1 terminal stock prices from the formula above, and the derivative's known payoff at each. Then step backward one level at a time, applying Lesson 1's one-step formula at every node in that level, using each node's two children one step ahead. Repeat until only the root node, today's price, remains.

body.text: One detail makes this cheaper than it looks. The risk-neutral probability p depends only on u, d, r, and delta-t, all fixed for the whole tree, so it is computed exactly once and reused at every single node, at every level, all the way back to the root. Nothing about backward induction ever asks for a different p depending on where a node sits in the tree.

children.text: Extend Lessons 1 and 2's exact setup, S0 = ₹100, u = 1.2, d = 0.9, r = 5% continuous per step, a ₹100-strike call, out to three steps instead of one. The single risk-neutral probability, p = 0.5042, carries over unchanged and gets reused at every node below.

body.caption: Terminal nodes after three steps (only 4, not 2^3 = 8)
Stepping backward, one level at a time

body.label: Three-step call price
body.context: Reached by applying the exact same one-step formula from Lesson 1 six times, once per node across the two intermediate levels plus the root, always with the same p

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A recombining binomial tree has 50 steps. How many distinct terminal stock prices does it have?
options: 2^50, since each step doubles the number of branches
51, since only the count of up-moves out of 50 steps matters, not their order
It depends on the specific values of u and d chosen
body.explanation: A recombining tree has N + 1 terminal nodes after N steps, here 51, because only the number of up-moves matters, never the sequence they occurred in. This is what keeps a 50-step, or a 126-step, tree computationally trivial instead of astronomically large.

body.title: A Non-Recombining Model
body.scenario: A junior quant is building a model where the up and down move sizes are allowed to depend on the stock's full price history, not just its current level, on the theory that this captures market behaviour more realistically.
body.prompt: What happens to the computational cost of this model as the number of steps grows, and why?
body.modelAnswer: If the up and down moves depend on the full path rather than just the current price, an up-then-down move and a down-then-up move are no longer guaranteed to land on the same price, so the tree stops recombining. Without recombination, the number of distinct terminal nodes reverts to 2 to the power N, exploding exponentially exactly as the naive count at the start of this lesson did. A model like this might capture something real, but it would need a fundamentally different, far more expensive computational approach, closer to Monte Carlo simulation from Chapter 1's method map than to a standard binomial tree, well beyond a few dozen steps.

body.text: A binomial tree stays computationally practical for one structural reason: constant up and down factors make it recombine, turning 2 to the power N possible paths into just N plus 1 distinct prices. Lose that property and the entire method stops being tractable.

points: A naive tree where every step branches independently produces 2^N distinct outcomes after N steps, computationally impossible well before N reaches the hundreds.
Using the same u and d at every step makes the tree recombine: an up-then-down move and a down-then-up move land on the identical price, S0 u^j d^(N-j).
Recombination means only N + 1 distinct terminal prices exist after N steps, not 2^N, which is the entire reason binomial trees are computationally practical.
Multi-step pricing is backward induction: compute the N + 1 terminal payoffs, then apply the one-step formula level by level back to today, reusing the same risk-neutral probability p at every node.
A three-step extension of the running ₹100 stock example, u = 1.2, d = 0.9, r = 5%, prices a ₹100-strike call at ₹17.67, computed with exactly six applications of Lesson 1's formula.
